item.content:encoded:
What makes a good teacher? Beyond knowing a subject, a good teacher can understand students, inspire confidence, and help young people discover what they are capable of becoming.

It was this broader responsibility of educators that Dr. Tunji Olowolafe explored while delivering the 2026 Convocation Lecture at the Sikiru Adetona College of Education, Science and Technology (SACOETEC), Omu-Ajose, Ogun State.

Speaking on Monday, 23 November 2026, on the theme “The Dual-Mandate NCE-Degree Programme: Prospects, Challenges and the Future of Teacher Education in Nigeria,” he described the programme as an important opportunity to reposition teacher education.

For decades, Colleges of Education depended on university affiliations to award Bachelor’s degrees, despite many possessing the academic capacity to run such programmes. The Federal Colleges of Education Act 2023 changed this, empowering eligible institutions to award degrees independently.

Under the Dual-Mandate programme, students can complete three years of NCE training and proceed to another two years for a Bachelor’s degree in Education.

Dr. Olowolafe explained that combining practical teaching skills with deeper academic knowledge would produce better-prepared educators. However, he cautioned that institutional autonomy must be supported by sustained funding, improved curricula and professional development.

With Nigeria facing an estimated shortage of one million teachers, he also called for greater integration of vocational education, artificial intelligence and digital skills into learning.

“AI can explain a quadratic equation at midnight, but it cannot offer the steady, empathetic guidance of a caring adult,” he said, emphasizing that artificial intelligence must complement, not replace, the human qualities of effective teaching.

During the lecture, Dr. Olowolafe announced that the Tunji Olowolafe Foundation would establish a fully equipped, solar-powered  Gbemisola Olowolafe Memorial ICT Centre (GOMTECH) with high-speed internet connectivity at SACOETEC.

The Foundation is also committed to recognising academic excellence and outstanding teaching at the College. This includes recognising the College’s first-class degree graduates and NCE distinction holders, alongside the overall best NCE and degree graduates. Lecturers, selected based on student ratings, will also be honoured for their teaching contributions. 

The initiative builds on the Foundation’s existing investment in education, including Project Digi-Teach at Ekiti State University and GOMTECH in Are-Ekiti.

For Dr. Olowolafe, the commitment to educators is also deeply personal. His mother was a teacher, his elder sister taught for years at Baptist Academy, Lagos, and his late wife, Gbemisola Olowolafe, was a lifelong educator.

He recalled the influence of teachers who shaped his own experience, particularly Mr. Soewu of Methodist Boys’ High School, whose patience helped students understand difficult concepts without humiliation.

Addressing the graduating class, he encouraged students to embrace lifelong learning and recognise that their qualifications could take them beyond conventional career paths.

“Your training is a launchpad, not a ceiling,” he said.

item.title: Remembering Pete Edochie: 5 Films That Made Him a Nollywood Legend
item.dc:creator: BellaNaija.com
item.description:
Veteran Nollywood actor Chief Dr Pete Edochie, MON, passed away in Enugu on Wednesday, 25 November 2026, at age 79, leaving behind an iconic screen legacy from Things Fall Apart to Lionheart.

The post Remembering Pete Edochie: 5 Films That Made Him a Nollywood Legend appeared first on BellaNaija - Showcasing Africa to the world. Read today!.
item.content:encoded:
Nollywood icon Pete Edochie, MON, who passed away at the age of 79 in Enugu.

Did you grow up watching Pete Edochie in Nollywood films? Then you probably remember that voice. Deep, commanding and unmistakable, it often came with his signature red cap, traditional Igbo attire and a generous helping of proverbs. The actor was just as memorable away from the screen, where his sharp wit, outspoken nature and candid opinions made him a fascinating personality in interviews. He was never one to shy away from saying exactly what he thought, and that straightforwardness became another part of what audiences remembered about him.

For generations of Nollywood viewers, Pete Edochie was the actor they could recognise before he had even finished his first sentence. He became one of Nigerian cinema’s most familiar faces, often playing kings, chiefs, fathers and respected elders. His breakthrough came in 1987 when he portrayed Okonkwo in the television adaptation of Chinua Achebe‘s Things Fall Apart, a performance that helped establish him as one of Nollywood’s most respected actors.

The veteran actor passed away in Enugu yesterday, on Wednesday, 25 November 2026, at the age of 79, following a prolonged battle with prostate cancer. Born in Zaria and originally from Ifite Nteje in Anambra State, Edochie began his career in broadcasting in 1967, eventually rising to become Deputy Managing Director of the Anambra Broadcasting Service. He went on to feature in hundreds of films, including Igodo, The Egg of Life and Lionheart.

Pete Edochie and Genevieve Nnaji behind the scenes on the set of the 2018 film Lionheart, where they played father and daughter Chief Ernest Obiagu and Adaeze Obiagu.

Survived by his wife, Josephine, and their six children, including actors Linc and Yul Edochie, he leaves behind a remarkable body of work. As we remember his life and contribution to Nigerian cinema, here are five films that capture some of the performances that made Pete Edochie a household name.

Things Fall Apart (1987)

Before Nollywood’s home-video boom even began, Pete Edochie became a household name across Nigeria and internationally through his breakout role as Okonkwo in the Nigerian Television Authority (NTA) adaptation of Chinua Achebe’s classic novel Things Fall Apart. Directed by David Orere, the acclaimed television miniseries marked Edochie’s first professional acting role and saw him bring the proud, fierce, and deeply conflicted Umuofia warrior to life with remarkable nuance. His performance was so transformative that, for generations of viewers, Edochie and Okonkwo became inseparable.

Rituals (1997)

As Nollywood entered its golden home-video era in the late 1990s, Edochie starred in Andy Amenechi’s gripping thriller Rituals as Don Pedro, a calculating member of a secretive and ruthless society. Trading his traditional royal regalia for sharp corporate power plays, Edochie anchored a cautionary drama about unchecked political ambition, greed, and moral compromise. His cool, authoritative delivery alongside co-stars including Richard Mofe–Damijo, Bob–Manuel Udokwu, and Eucharia Anunobi made the film one of the defining Nollywood thrillers of the decade.

Igodo: The Land of the Living Dead (1999)

In this landmark supernatural adventure directed by Andy Amenechi and Don Pedro Obaseki, Edochie played one of the principal elders guiding a cursed community desperate for salvation. The story follows seven chosen warriors sent into a perilous evil forest to retrieve a mystical sword capable of breaking the land’s curse. Sharing the screen with Sam Dede, Norbert Young, and Charles Okafor, Edochie grounded the high-stakes fantasy with his signature gravitas and mastery of Igbo proverbs.

Veteran Nollywood actor Chief Dr Pete Edochie and his wife, Barrister Mrs Josephine Edochie, at a church service.

Egg of Life (2003)

Directed by Andy Amenechi, Egg of Life stands out as one of early-2000s Nollywood’s most beloved fantasy epics, with Edochie cast as the Igwe whose kingdom is thrown into crisis when his young heir falls gravely ill.When the chief priestess—played by Clarion Chukwura—reveals that only a sacred egg hidden deep within a spirit-guarded forest can save the prince’s life, a group of maidens embarks on a perilous quest. Edochie’s dignified portrayal of a father and monarch balancing royal duty with quiet vulnerability gave the film its emotional core.

Lionheart (2018)

For a younger global audience, Edochie’s performance as Chief Ernest Obiagu in Genevieve Nnaji’s directorial debut Lionheart remains one of his most endearing screen appearances. Playing the respected founder of Lionheart Transport Company who is forced to step back due to health challenges, Edochie brought warmth, humour, and quiet wisdom to a modern family drama co-starring Genevieve Nnaji, Nkem Owoh, and Onyeka Onwenu. Released worldwide on Netflix in 2019, the film showcased his effortless transition into contemporary cinema.

item.content:encoded:
In a powerful demonstration of its commitment to Africa’s digital and economic future, Zenith Bank has concluded Zecathon 6.0, its flagship startup competition and innovation program. Executed by Beyond Limits Global as its implementation partner, the competition deployed a staggering ₦190 Million in non-equity capital across three strategic tracks, reinforcing its position as a critical launchpad for the continent’s tech ecosystem.

​A Holistic Investment in The Innovation Pipeline

This year’s event drew thousands of applications across Africa and introduced a wider, more inclusive format. The competition successfully spanned the entire innovation pipeline—from brilliant secondary school students testing their first ideas to seasoned developers building advanced AI architectures, and growth-stage startups ready to scale their market footprints.

​In her welcome remarks at the 2026 Zenith Bank Tech Fair, Dame Dr. Adaora Umeoji, OON, Group Managing Director/Chief Executive Officer of Zenith Bank Plc, said:

“The next generation of global AI champions can and should come from Africa. This is why the Zecathon sits at the heart of this Tech Fair. It is our search for Africa’s most promising innovators, across every sector, and our commitment is to support them with capital, mentorship and incubation.”

Echoing this commitment, Lanre Oladimeji, General Manager at Zenith Bank & MD of Finopay, noted the strategic necessity of the platform.

“The financial services sector thrives on continuous evolution. The solutions presented across these tracks—from inclusive voice-first banking to digital procurement platforms—are the exact kind of robust, user-centric technologies that will shape the next generation of our digital economy.”

​“Zecathon 6.0 represents a deliberate investment in the depth and long-term potential of Africa’s innovation ecosystem. Beyond creating a platform for showcasing ideas, it is about strengthening the connections between talent, technology, entrepreneurship and industry, and creating pathways for innovation to translate into tangible economic and social value. Ultimately, the ambition is to build an ecosystem where innovation can thrive, businesses can grow and solutions can create lasting impact,” said Fikun Aluko, Innovation Expert and Co-lead of the Zecathon 6.0 Program.

Expanding on the program’s design and execution, Daniel Iyiola, Program Manager at Beyond Limits Global, said:

“Zecathon 6.0 was designed around a deliberate approach to engaging innovation at different stages of development. The Startup Pitch Competition challenged growth-stage businesses to demonstrate commercial traction, market relevance and the capacity to scale. The Innovation Hackathon placed emphasis on applied problem-solving, technical execution and the development of working solutions to real-world challenges, while the Future Innovators Challenge created an avenue for senior secondary school students to engage with technology, creativity and innovation from an early stage. Bringing these distinct pathways together allowed the program to recognise established innovation, test emerging solutions and nurture the next generation of talent.”

​Startup Pitch Competition: Accelerating Growth-Stage Ventures

The Startup Pitch Competition saw fierce competition among 21 semi-finalists drawn from a pool of 1,609 African applicants. The ₦90 million prize pool for this track was led by Cutstruct Technology Limited, which secured ₦35 million for an innovative digital procurement platform seamlessly connecting developers, contractors, and financiers in the construction sector.

​The top five was completed by ventures demonstrating high-impact solutions across key economic sectors: Sproutly (₦20 million) for a financial infrastructure platform helping schools manage operations and fee payments; PharmaRun (₦15 million) for a technology-powered network ensuring last-mile medication access; AUI BRAND (₦10 million) for locally manufactured, deep-tech medical equipment aimed at reducing newborn mortality; and ProDevs (₦10 million) for an AI-powered HR platform streamlining global hiring.

​Innovation Hackathon: Engineering the Future of Finance

Bringing an unprecedented level of technical rigor to the event, the Innovation Hackathon tasked developers with solving complex banking challenges. Twenty shortlisted teams out of 1,213 applicants participated in an intense three-day, in-person coding sprint.

​The ₦90 million hackathon prize pool was topped by Team Solo, winning ₦35 million for engineering a highly inclusive banking application featuring customizable voice and sign-language modes for diverse accessibility needs. 10x Brains secured ₦20 million for an instant fraud-prevention verification layer, and Rumour Hunters won ₦15 million for an AI-driven transaction diagnostic platform. Òmìnira (₦10 million) and Team Avera (₦10 million) were also rewarded for pioneering a voice-first accessibility tool with sonar selfies and building an autonomous AI incident laboratory, respectively.

Future Innovators Challenge: Empowering the Next Generation

Ensuring the pipeline of future talent remains robust, the Future Innovators Challenge tasked senior secondary school students with developing community-driven solutions. Following an intensive three-day design-thinking bootcamp and final showcase, three brilliant schools emerged victorious from a pool of 114 applications, sharing a ₦10 million prize pool.

Caleb British International School, Lagos, emerged as the overall winner, claiming ₦5 million for ReLearn, a technology-enabled textbook recovery platform giving unused books a second life. Queen of the Rosary College, Onitsha, secured second place (₦3 million) for SabiCare, a gamified platform teaching life-saving first aid through story-based simulations. Regina Pacis International Secondary School, Onitsha, came third (₦2 million) for FireHearts, an IoT-powered safety system designed to detect dangerous gas leaks and prevent household fires.

Beyond the Capital: Building Sustainable Enterprises

To ensure these solutions transition from competition winners to sustainable, market-ready enterprises, the top teams from the Hackathon and Business Pitch tracks will undergo a rigorous two-week development program. This post-event accelerator is designed to complement their financial backing with executive leadership training, ecosystem networking, and technical refinement.

For more updates, visit and follow @zenithbankplc and @the_beyondlimits on social media.

item.content:encoded:
Close-up of a woman brushing her teeth as part of her daily dental hygiene routine. Image by PNW Production for Pexels

A toothbrush with fluoride toothpaste is the better choice for protecting your teeth against cavities, but chewing sticks are real cleaning tools too. Some studies have found that using a chewing stick alongside brushing can help remove more plaque and reduce gum inflammation. So if you grew up with a chewing stick, you do not need to feel embarrassed about it.

Can a chewing stick clean your teeth as well as a toothbrush?

In studies with adults, certain chewing sticks can clean your teeth about as well as a toothbrush for plaque and gum health, as long as you use them properly. Plaque is the soft, sticky layer of bacteria that builds up on your teeth, and it can lead to gum disease and cavities.

Studies of miswak, a type of chewing stick made from the Salvadora persica tree, have found that it can remove plaque and reduce gum inflammation about as effectively as a toothbrush. Some studies also found that people who used miswak alongside brushing had less plaque and less gum inflammation than people who only brushed.

Nigerian chewing sticks come from many plants, including dogonyaro (neem) and orogbo (bitter kola). Not every type has been studied, so we cannot assume they all produce the same results.

Why do dentists recommend a toothbrush with fluoride toothpaste?

Dentists recommend a toothbrush with fluoride toothpaste because it protects against cavities, and a chewing stick cannot promise that. Fluoride toothpaste is proven to reduce tooth decay compared with toothpaste without fluoride. The American Dental Association recommends brushing twice a day with it.

The chewing stick studies discussed measured plaque and gum health, not cavities. Unlike fluoride toothpaste, a chewing stick doesn’t provide a reliable amount of fluoride to help protect your teeth against decay.

A toothbrush typically reaches the inner surfaces of your teeth more effectively because the bristles are aligned with the handle.

The best routine is to brush twice a day with fluoride toothpaste and use your chewing stick as an extra if you like it. Clean between your teeth once a day with floss or an interdental brush, which is a tiny brush made for the gaps between teeth. Neither a chewing stick nor a toothbrush fully cleans those spaces.

How do you use a chewing stick without hurting your gums?

If you’re to use a chewing stick, use it gently and keep it fresh. First, peel back about half an inch of bark and chew the tip until it frays soft like a brush.

Then clean with short strokes moving away from the gum, because hard side-to-side scrubbing can irritate your gums. Replace the tip when it becomes worn or stiff, since a rough tip is harder on your gums, and keep your strokes light.

When you have a tooth problem, always tell your dentist exactly what you use so they can give you advice that fits your routine. You could say, “I use a chewing stick most mornings, and I also brush with toothpaste. Can you check my teeth and gums and show me if there’s anything I should change?”

If you notice bleeding gums, sensitivity near your gumline or gums that seem to be pulling back, book a dental check-up. These symptoms can have different causes, and your dentist can help identify what’s happening. Whichever one you use, you are allowed to mention it to your dentist.

The four-part series, also starring Jim Iyke, Seun Ajayi and Folu Storms, is now streaming exclusively on KAVA.

An illicit affair threatens to upend the life of a successful tech entrepreneur in the final trailer for Spiraling, the Nigerian psychological thriller from creator and director Wande Thomas, unveiled to coincide with the series’ streaming debut.

Toni Tones (King of Boys, The Smart Money Woman) stars as Sade, a woman whose professional success and carefully curated personal life begin to unravel following a single lapse in judgment. Against the backdrop of a historic election, what starts as a private indiscretion escalates into a web of deception, betrayal and unprecedented consequences.

Jim Iyke (Bad Comments, Merry Men 2), Seun Ajayi (Japa, The Smart Money Woman) and Folu Storms (Red Circle, Baby Farm) round out the principal cast.

A new series of character posters has also been released alongside the final trailer, spotlighting the key players in the psychological thriller.

Exploring the intersection of ambition, desire and power, the series examines the lengths people will go to protect their reputations, and what happens when they can no longer control the narrative.

Spiraling is created and directed by Thomas, who also produces alongside Isoken Ogiemwonyi under their respective production banners, Urbangidi Showtime and Studio Ogiso.

The four-part thriller marks the latest addition to KAVA’s growing slate of straight to series African scripted entertainment.

item.content:encoded:
After more than 30 years of experience in the fashion industry, the entrepreneur is bringing her experience to a Nigerian clothing brand built on a simple proposition: quality should not have to come at an exorbitant price.

In fashion, the conversation often begins with style, but it rarely ends there. Quality, affordability, accessibility and the story behind what we wear are increasingly becoming part of how consumers make their choices. For Alero Ebigbeyi, these are not just considerations; they are the principles shaping her latest venture, HÉYCH.

The Nigerian fashion and clothing brand officially opened its retail store on November 10, bringing together fashion enthusiasts, media executives, influencers, friends and industry personalities for an introduction to the brand and its collections. Guests explored the space, examined the clothing and made purchases. Yet, amid the excitement of the launch, two observations kept coming up: the quality of the pieces and their affordability.

It was a response that reflected the thinking behind HÉYCH, a brand seeking to occupy an important space in the market by making well-made, stylish clothing accessible without asking consumers to compromise on quality.

For Ebigbeyi, this approach is informed by more than three decades of experience in the fashion industry. Having spent over 30 years understanding the business of clothing, she brings to HÉYCH a perspective that extends beyond trends and aesthetics to the practical realities of production, pricing and delivering value.

“One thing that sets HÉYCH apart is that we do not compromise on quality, and we are equally intentional about making our products affordable. With over 30 years of experience in this industry, I understand the importance of quality, production standards and delivering value to customers,” she says.

Rethinking How Fashion Is Produced

That understanding is reflected in one of the brand’s most significant decisions: its investment in local manufacturing.

Behind HÉYCH’s retail offering is a manufacturing facility in Lagos, a strategic investment that gives the brand greater control over production while creating the capacity to fulfil orders in large quantities.

For Ebigbeyi, local production is as much about business efficiency as it is about building something sustainable within Nigeria.

Importation can introduce several layers of cost and complexity, from logistics and shipping to delays and quality-control challenges. Producing locally offers an opportunity to reduce some of these constraints, exercise closer oversight of production and create a more direct relationship between the manufacturer and the customer.

“Establishing our production facility here in Lagos is a deliberate business decision. Local manufacturing allows us to eliminate many of the bottlenecks associated with importing clothing, reduce unnecessary costs and maintain better control over the quality of what we produce. We want our customers to enjoy excellent products without having to pay unnecessarily high prices,” she explains.

It is an approach that also gives HÉYCH a broader commercial outlook. Beyond individual retail customers, the brand is positioning its production capacity to serve churches, concert organisers, corporate organisations, event producers and other brands that require clothing in substantial quantities.

For these clients, working with a local manufacturer can offer greater flexibility, closer communication and the opportunity to carry out quality checks during production. It also creates an alternative to sourcing large clothing orders from overseas markets, particularly when customisation, timelines and consistency are important.

Fashion, Business and the Value of Local Enterprise

There is a larger conversation taking place around Nigeria’s fashion industry, particularly the need to strengthen local production and create more opportunities within the country’s creative and manufacturing sectors.

While Nigerian designers and fashion brands have earned recognition for their creativity, the infrastructure required to support production at scale remains an important part of the industry’s development. HÉYCH’s model brings this conversation into focus by connecting retail fashion with manufacturing capacity.

The benefits also extend beyond the products themselves. Local production creates employment opportunities and supports the people and processes involved in turning clothing concepts into finished products. For Ebigbeyi, building HÉYCH is therefore about creating a business that can deliver commercial value while contributing to the local economy.

This is perhaps what makes the brand’s proposition interesting. It is not simply about encouraging consumers to buy Nigerian-made clothing; it is about demonstrating that locally produced fashion can be commercially competitive, quality-conscious and accessible.

A Brand with More Than One Ambition

The opening of the HÉYCH retail store marks an important step in introducing the brand to a wider audience, but its ambitions extend beyond the retail experience. By combining a consumer-facing fashion offering with the capacity for large-scale production, the brand is exploring two connected opportunities within the Nigerian market.

For Ebigbeyi, the direction is clear: build a brand that understands what customers want, respects the importance of quality and recognises that affordability must be part of the equation.

With more than 30 years of industry experience informing its direction, HÉYCH enters the market with a proposition that speaks to both the everyday fashion consumer and organisations looking for a dependable local clothing production partner.

Ultimately, its story is part of a wider question about the future of Nigerian fashion: how can the industry move beyond creativity to build stronger production capabilities, create jobs and make quality clothing more accessible?

For Alero Ebigbeyi, HÉYCH is one answer to that question.

About HÉYCH

HÉYCH is a Nigerian fashion and clothing brand committed to delivering quality, style and affordability through locally driven production. With a retail store and manufacturing facility in Lagos, the brand serves individual customers, institutions, corporate organisations, churches, concert organisers and other clients requiring clothing in large quantities.

Every outfit featured in this post is proudly HÉYCH!

There’s something beautiful waiting for you.

And, of course, no celebration would be complete without a little indulgence. Guests can also look forward to delicious milk treats from Kerrygold, adding a taste of the brand to the day’s festivities.

Beyond the fun and entertainment, Milk & Magic Christmas Fest reflects Kerrygold’s commitment to creating meaningful connections with consumers beyond the products they enjoy every day. By bringing families together in a relaxed and engaging setting, the festival offers an opportunity to experience the brand in a different way, while celebrating the simple pleasures of good food and shared moments.

With its distinctive rich, creamy taste and proud Irish dairy heritage, Kerrygold continues to bring quality dairy experiences closer to Nigerian consumers. Through its products and consumer engagement initiatives, the brand remains focused on creating experiences that resonate with its consumers and bring people together.

As the countdown to Christmas begins, Milk & Magic Christmas Fest promises a lovely opportunity for families to share in the excitement of the season, enjoy some festive treats and make memories that will last beyond the holidays.

item.content:encoded:
Super Falcons striker Asisat Oshoala in her graduation gown and cap at Wembley Stadium after earning her MSc in International Sports Management.

Super Falcons striker Asisat Oshoala has added a brand-new title to her name—and this time, it comes with a graduation cap and gown.

The Nigerian football star graduated today, Wednesday, 25 November 2026, with a Master of Science (MSc) degree in International Sports Management from the Global Institute of Sport (GIS) at a ceremony held at Wembley Stadium in London. Sharing photos from the graduation on her Instagram Story, the forward kept her caption short, sweet, and full of charm: “I don finally make my mama proud.”

Long before collecting European trophies and continental awards, the Ikorodu-born athlete attended Aunty Ayo International School in Lagos, where she first started playing football before pursuing the sport professionally. Now, alongside her playing career, she holds a postgraduate master’s degree in sports management—equipping herself for leadership roles off the pitch as well as on it.

Asisat Oshoala holds two bouquets of flowers while celebrating her Global Institute of Sport graduation at Wembley Stadium.

On the field, Oshoala remains one of Africa’s most decorated footballers. Playing primarily as a centre-forward—and occasionally out wide as a winger—the 32-year-old represents Nigeria on the international stage as a key pillar of the Super Falcons, and currently plays club football in the Saudi Women’s Premier League for Al-Hilal, following spells with Arsenal, Liverpool, Dalian Quanjian, FC Barcelona Femení, and Bay FC.

Her footballing CV speaks for itself. A six-time CAF African Women’s Footballer of the Year—the first player in history to win the honour six times—Oshoala has won multiple UEFA Women’s Champions League trophies with Barcelona, claimed Liga F and Women’s Super League titles, and represented Nigeria across multiple FIFA Women’s World Cups and Olympic Games. Beyond football, she also runs the Asisat Oshoala Academy and Foundation, which empowers young girls in Nigeria through sports and education.

item.title: Meet Funmi Ojo, the University of Ibadan Graduate Who Earned a Perfect 7.0 CGPA
item.dc:creator: BellaNaija.com
item.description:
Cosmetic Scientist Funmi Ojo emerged as Best Graduating Student in Pharmaceutics and Industrial Pharmacy at the University of Ibadan with a 7.0/7.0 MSc CGPA while running her business and building a laboratory.

The post Meet Funmi Ojo, the University of Ibadan Graduate Who Earned a Perfect 7.0 CGPA appeared first on BellaNaija - Showcasing Africa to the world. Read today!.
item.content:encoded:
Doctoral scholar and University of Ibadan alumna Funmi Ojo.

There are academic achievements that make you admire a person’s brilliance, and then there are stories that make you think about what determination, self-belief and a second chance can make possible. For Funmi Ojo, earning a perfect CGPA of 7.0/7.0 was about more than getting excellent grades. It was a promise she had made to herself, one shaped by an undergraduate experience in which she felt she had not quite lived up to her own academic potential. This time, she was determined to give herself nothing less than her very best.

And she did. Funmi emerged as the Best Graduating Student in the Department of Pharmaceutics and Industrial Pharmacy at the University of Ibadan for the 2024/2025 academic session, completing her MSc in Drug Formulation Science with a perfect 7.0/7.0 CGPA. A Cosmetic Scientist with a B.Pharm from the same university, she is now a doctoral scholar, taking her academic journey into its next chapter.

But how do you pursue a perfect score while running a growing business, building a laboratory and making room for the other parts of your life? In this interview with BellaNaija, Funmi talks about the decision to aim for a perfect CGPA from the very beginning, the study systems that helped her get there, and the lessons she learnt about time management, discipline and making the most of every mark. She also shares her thoughts on using AI as a learning tool, tackling difficult courses and knowing when to put everything else aside and focus on the goal.

At what point did you realise you were chasing a record-breaking grade? Was it a goal from Day 1, or did it evolve?

It was a goal from day one. About three weeks into my MSc programme, I had already decided that I wanted a perfect score. I felt I owed it to myself, particularly because I hadn’t achieved the first-class degree I wanted during my undergraduate years. It took getting to 300 level before I became more intentional about my academics, and by then, I realised I was capable of getting excellent grades. I had also seen how much strong academic results could change the trajectory of some of my colleagues, and I didn’t want to feel that I had shortchanged myself. I knew I wanted to get it right this time.

Funmi Ojo, Best Graduating Student in the Department of Pharmaceutics and Industrial Pharmacy at the University of Ibadan.

Interestingly, my MSc years were also when I took my business most seriously. It was growing rapidly, and I was building my own laboratory, so I had quite a lot to manage alongside my studies. During my undergraduate years, I sometimes blamed my business commitments for my academic performance, but I later realised that I had to learn how to manage my time better. I became more intentional about how I used each hour and stopped making excuses for the things I wanted to achieve. By the time my responsibilities increased towards the end of the programme, I had already laid the groundwork and knew how to allocate my time.

Explain your systems. Beyond “reading hard,” what specific study techniques or daily schedules kept you at the top?

I think there are five systems that really made the difference for me.

  • Every mark counts. Don’t wait until examinations before taking your academics seriously. Attendance, laboratory work, continuous assessments, presentations and assignments all contribute to your final grade. It’s often easier to secure 36 out of 40 in your CA than to get 60 out of 60 in an examination. I take every opportunity to earn those marks seriously, especially presentations, which are usually one of my strengths. Those marks can make a real difference.
  • Use AI as a learning tool. AI is one of the biggest advantages students of our generation have. You can upload lecture slides, ask it to explain difficult concepts, provide examples, summarise lengthy materials and generate probable examination questions. Think of it as having a tutorial you can interact with and ask to explain things in a way you understand.
  • Understand that academia is systemic. Knowing something isn’t enough; you also need to retain, recall and communicate it effectively. One of the ways I do this is by teaching others. If you can explain a difficult concept to someone with no background knowledge of the subject, it usually means you understand it yourself.
  • Learn how to answer questions, not just how to read. I think examinations are about 60% knowledge and 40% diction. You need to communicate what you know clearly. I read widely, practise past questions and organise my answers so that my lecturers can follow my thinking.
  • Lock in during examination weeks. A strict daily study routine isn’t always practical when you’re running a business or juggling other responsibilities. So, I maximise the marks available throughout the semester, then give examinations my full attention for those two or three weeks. I temporarily put social activities aside, knowing I can return to them afterwards.

Cosmetic Scientist and University of Ibadan graduate Funmi Ojo in a blush pink tweed two-piece outfit.

What did you have to sacrifice? Tell us about the social events, personal time, hobbies or even sleep you had to put aside to protect your CGPA.

I live a very well-rounded life. I go to the gym, spend time with friends, enjoy my hobbies, read and run a business. So, I wouldn’t necessarily say I sacrificed having a life to achieve my grades. I think it’s more about understanding that certain seasons require you to temporarily put some things aside. During the semester, I make time for my business, friends and other interests while ensuring I secure the 40 marks available outside the final examination. But when examinations come around, I’m completely locked in. For those two or three weeks, I’m not going out or attending social events. If you know me during examination season, you probably cannot call me to do anything else! Once my examinations are over, I go right back to enjoying my life.

Funmi Ojo’s University of Ibadan Postgraduate College certificate scroll tube confirming her 2024/2025 PGC Doctoral Scholar award.

This is particularly important because I run a business, and work doesn’t simply stop because I have examinations. There are clients, production schedules, employees and other responsibilities to manage. So, I have to be deliberate about scheduling my working hours and creating dedicated time for studying. Ultimately, I don’t think having multiple responsibilities means everything else has to suffer. It’s about understanding your priorities, knowing when each one needs your attention and recognising when it’s time to temporarily pull back. For me, that period is usually the two or three weeks of examinations.

How did you handle the toughest courses or departmental hurdles that usually break a student’s GPA?

I studied Pharmacy, so there was quite a bit of mathematics and science involved. The funny thing is, I don’t particularly like mathematics. I love chemistry, manufacturing and production, but mathematics? Not so much! I already knew it wasn’t a subject that came naturally to me, so I made sure to give those courses extra attention. My auntie, who is a schoolteacher, always used to tell us that no subject is inherently difficult; sometimes, it’s simply a subject you haven’t read enough or don’t particularly enjoy. I’ve carried that mentality with me because I believe there’s very little you cannot learn if you’re willing to put in the time and effort.

Funmi Ojo celebrating her MSc graduation from the University of Ibadan with a 7.0/7.0 CGPA.

I think it’s important to identify your difficult courses early rather than spend all your time on subjects you’re already good at. Those challenging courses can make or break your CGPA, so you have to give them the attention they need. For me, that meant revisiting difficult topics, practising and reading until I understood them. I also think the lecturer’s teaching style matters. Attending classes helps you understand their expectations and how they approach examinations. Sometimes, you have to adjust your study methods to suit a particular course or lecturer. Ultimately, you cannot keep avoiding a subject because you don’t enjoy it. You have to identify what isn’t working, find another way to approach it and keep at it until you understand.

What habits, routines, or mindset helped you stay consistent throughout your university journey, and what practical advice would you pass on to students who hope to follow a similar path?

I wouldn’t say I’m the biggest stickler for habits and routines—I have ADHD, so sticking to rigid routines can be difficult for me. What has helped me most is my mindset and what I’ve internalised about education, hard work and my abilities. I believe that no subject is inherently too difficult and that you can understand almost anything if you’re willing to put in the work. I also believe education is one of the most accessible ways to improve your circumstances, especially if you don’t come from much.

I say this as someone who has built a business and experienced the demands of working in the real world. In many ways, reading hard is a little easier than working hard! Running a business comes with variables outside your control, from people and capital to customers and market conditions. With academics, the process is more straightforward: you have your books, learning materials and examinations, and a clearer idea of what you need to do to improve. You have to believe that education can take you places and that the effort you put in today can change the trajectory of your life.

Funmi Ojo, Best Graduating Student in the Department of Pharmaceutics and Industrial Pharmacy at the University of Ibadan.

My practical advice is to take every mark seriously, use AI as a learning tool, find ways to retain and communicate what you’ve learnt, and give difficult courses extra attention. When examinations come around, lock in and give them your best. Above all, don’t wait until you feel motivated or convince yourself that some people are simply born brilliant. Believe that what you’re working towards is worth the effort, because it is.

And I think if you can internalise that, develop the right approach to your studies and consistently put in the work, you’ll be just fine.

item.content:encoded:
The fifth edition of Entertainment Week Africa brought together filmmakers, musicians, designers, artists, tech founders, investors, mentors, policymakers and fans for six days of screenings, showcases, masterclasses and celebrations under the theme Five Years of Closing the Gap.

People from 121 countries and territories applied to speak, attend or screen their work, and more than 19,000 people joined the programme in person and online, as EWA streamed its sessions live for the first time. Over the six days, more than 150 speakers led nearly 100 panels, masterclasses, workshops, roundtables and podcast sessions, while around 50 films were screened across the week.

The celebrations began on Opening Night at the Livespot Entertarium, where guests were treated to an evening of music, fashion, film and comedy to mark five years of EWA. Sixteen emerging artists performed in front of a room of industry leaders, creatives and partners, and the night featured an exclusive 30-minute screening of University of Side Hustle, the first scripted feature film from Livespot Studios, written by Dami Elebe and executive produced by Deola Art Alade.

By day, EbonyLife Place hosted a packed programme across seven tracks: Film & TV; Music; Fashion & Beauty; AI & Tech; Art & Animation; Live Events & Production; and Creative Enterprise. Nissi Ogulu led a masterclass on animation as Africa’s next big storytelling frontier, and From Lagos to Disney explored what it takes to bring African stories to global screens. Creators picked up practical tips in sessions with Victoire, Ifeoma Udeme and Canva. Other sessions tackled sync licensing, music funding, building Africa’s touring circuit and turning creative skills into businesses. The podcast stage kept the energy going with live recordings of CreativiTea and Crea8torium, which closed the final day.

Fashion took over the Entertarium for The Runway Coterie, an evening of bold collections that ended with the announcement of the EWA Fashion Lab winners after a week-long programme with mentors. Hooked By Lade won first place with ₦2 million, Estaz took second place and ₦1 million, and Melira placed third, winning ₦500,000. Lush Hair styled the runway as the show’s hair sponsor.

Next door, the EWA Art Floor invited guests into The Spaces Between Us, an exhibition that blended photography, painting, installation, archival work, fashion and live performance. Curated by Jumoke Sanwo and produced with Revolving Art Incubator (RAI) as it celebrated its tenth anniversary, the exhibition featured work by 21 Nigerian artists and seven fashion designers.

In the EWA Sound Lab, producers and songwriters spent time creating alongside Banx & Ranx, the Grammy-nominated, Juno Award-winning duo whose credits include records for Sean Paul, Dua Lipa and Ella Eyre. Filmmakers also had a dedicated moment in the spotlight as the British Council’s Film Lab Africa 2 Lagos Showcase premiered new work from its cohort of Nigerian screenwriters and creative producers.

The 2026 EWA Ambassadors, Qing Madi, Malik Afegbua, Juma Jux, Boubacar Jiba, Akin Faminu, Genoveva Umeh, Efa Iwara, Motolani Alake and Collins Sekaugo, represented the breadth of talent EWA brings together, from music and film to digital art, fashion and tech.

“Five years ago, we set out to build a home for African creativity, a place where talent is celebrated and given what it needs to go further,” said Deola Art Alade, Founder and Convener of Entertainment Week Africa. “This year, watching emerging artists, designers and filmmakers take their moment on our stages, with people tuning in from around the world, reminded us why we do this. African entertainment is having its moment, and we want to make sure the people behind it can build careers and businesses that last.”

That ambition also showed in the work behind the scenes, where the EWA Deal Room awarded ₦12 million in grants to creative and creative-tech startups, and around 30 mentors supported founders and designers throughout the week.

EWA 2026 was sponsored by Pepsi, MTN, The Singleton, Indomie and Lush Hair, alongside Livespot and Rent A Rig, with EbonyLife Place as the venue partner.

Entertainment Week Africa returns from 9–14 November 2027, and registration is open at ewafrica.com/apply. For news, opportunities and first looks at what’s coming next, subscribe at ewafrica.com/newsletter and follow @ewafrica_ on Instagram.

item.dc:creator: BellaNaija.com

Senegal captain Sadio Mané thanks Senegalese supporters and sends a message of respect to Morocco after the Court of Arbitration for Sport reinstated Senegal as 2025 AFCON champions.

item.content:encoded:
Senegal captain Sadio Mané and his teammates gather around the Africa Cup of Nations trophy on the pitch in Rabat.

Yesterday, after the Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS) overturned a previous Confederation of African Football (CAF) decision on Tuesday, 24 November 2026, and reinstated Senegal as the champions of the 2025 Africa Cup of Nations (AFCON), the 34-year-old Senegal captain Sadio Mané took to Instagram to celebrate the news. Alongside photos of himself and his teammates lifting the trophy, Mané thanked Senegalese supporters at home and in the diaspora, praised his squad for their sacrifices, and extended a thoughtful message of respect to Morocco.

If you’re just catching up on how the Teranga Lions arrived at this moment, the journey since the final in Rabat on 18 January 2026 has been anything but ordinary. During a tense stoppage-time spell—after Senegal had a goal disallowed and hosts Morocco were awarded a late penalty—Senegal’s coach Pape Thiaw pulled his players off the pitch, delaying the match for 14 minutes. It was Mané—widely celebrated as one of Africa’s finest footballers of his generation after trophy-laden spells with Liverpool and Bayern Munich before joining Al-Nassr—who stepped in to persuade his teammates to return and finish the game. Senegal went on to win 1–0 in extra time thanks to a Pape Gueye goal.

Senegal captain Sadio Mané raises the AFCON trophy on the podium alongside Édouard Mendy and the Teranga Lions squad.

In March, however, CAF’s Appeal Board overturned that result and awarded Morocco a 3–0 forfeit victory over the temporary walk-off. The Senegalese Football Federation appealed to CAS in Lausanne, and on Tuesday,sport’s highest court ruled unanimously in Senegal’s favour—confirming that Congolese referee Jean-Jacques Ndala acted within his authority when resuming the match, and restoring Senegal’s second AFCON title.

Read Mané’s full statement below:

The decision by the Court of Arbitration for Sport reinstating Senegal as champions of Africa fills us with joy. First, I want to thank the entire Senegalese people, both at home and in the diaspora. You supported us from the first match right through to this decision. Your trust gave us strength during the most difficult moments.

Thank you to my teammates. I know the effort and sacrifices each of you made to win this second star. I am proud to have experienced this journey alongside you. My thanks also go to the entire technical staff and everyone who supported the Lions.

I would also like to send a message of respect and encouragement to the Moroccan people and the Moroccan players. They had a great campaign and should be proud of what they achieved. I wish them all the best going forward. Senegal and Morocco are two brotherly nations. May the passion for football continue to bring us closer together.

Congratulations to all Senegalese people. This victory belongs to you too.

While the Royal Moroccan Football Federation has indicated it plans to challenge the decision further, CAF has confirmed it respects the CAS ruling.

Senegal captain Sadio Mané raises the Africa Cup of Nations trophy while lifted by teammates after the final in Rabat.

item.content:encoded:
Miss Universe Congo Jessi Kalambayi wearing her national crown and sash in a gold beaded evening gown. Photo Credit: Jessi Kalambayi/Instagram 

The 75th Miss Universe competition has come to a close in San Juan, Puerto Rico, and Jessi Kalambayi gave the Democratic Republic of the Congo a night to remember. Out of 116 contestants from around the world—and 17 representing Africa—the 28-year-old beauty queen became the sole African delegate to reach the Top 12 at Tuesday night’s live finale, representing her country as Miss Universe Congo at the Coliseo de Puerto Rico José Miguel Agrelot.

That is a major result for the Central African nation, and there is quite a story behind the woman who made it happen.

Born Jessi Longwe Kalambayi in Kinshasa and raised between South Africa and the United States, Jessi arrived at Miss Universe with an impressive background beyond pageantry. She holds a bachelor’s degree in Psychology with a minor in Africana Studies from Metropolitan State University of Denver, as well as a master’s degree in International Studies, specialising in Migration, from the University of Denver. Her professional experience includes working as a programme manager supporting refugee resettlement. She has also used her platform to speak about embracing natural African hair textures, from afros to braids, as part of celebrating Congolese identity.

Miss Universe Congo Jessi Kalambayi honours the Democratic Republic of the Congo national football team for her Miss Universe 2026 national costume. Photo Credit: Jessi Kalambayi/Instagram 

And this was hardly her first time navigating a major pageant stage. Before winning the Miss Universe DRC 2026 crown in July, succeeding Dorcas Dienda, Jessi had already made her mark in the United States. In 2024, she won Miss Colorado USA and went on to place in the Top 10 at Miss USA. That experience came in handy in San Juan, where she moved through the preliminary rounds and closed-door interviews with the nine-member selection committee to secure a place in the initial Top 30.

Miss Universe Congo Jessi Kalambayi on stage during the swimsuit round of the Miss Universe 2026 Preliminary Competition. Photo Credit: Jessi Kalambayi/Instagram 

Finale night brought another big moment. Alongside fellow African Top 30 semifinalists from Ethiopia, Guinea, Tanzania and Uganda, Jessi made it through the swimsuit round and advanced into the Top 12 alongside contestants from Puerto Rico, Venezuela, the Philippines, the United States and France—standing as Africa’s lone representative in that round.

Miss Universe Congo Jessi Kalambayi during the Top 12 evening gown round at the 75th Miss Universe finale in San Juan, Puerto Rico. Photo Credit: Jessi Kalambayi/Instagram 

Her Miss Universe journey came to an end just before the announcement of the Top 5, while Puerto Rico’s Jennifer Barreto went on to claim the crown. Still, Jessi’s run marked an important showing for the Democratic Republic of the Congo and closed out the 75th Miss Universe competition on a high note for the continent.

Miss Universe Congo Jessi Kalambayi steps out in a yellow sculptural gown ahead of the Miss Universe 2026 Preliminary Show in San Juan. Photo Credit: Jessi Kalambayi/Instagram

Cardi B‘s latest fashion moment comes with a lovely Nigerian connection, and we have two designers to celebrate! The rapper is the newest cover star of Billboard Canada, following her recognition as the inaugural Global Woman of the Year at the 2026 Billboard Canada Women in Music ceremony in Toronto on 24 November 2026. For the accompanying editorial, her longtime creative collaborator Kollin Carter worked with photographer AB+DM Studio to put together a series of looks, including two gorgeous creations from Nigerian fashion houses Weiz Dhurm Franklyn and Sevon Dejana. And BNers, both designers brought something very different to the spread.

First up is a sculptural blue mermaid gown by Abelia Anaba Franklyn, the creative mind behind Weiz Dhurm Franklyn. The design comes from the brand’s Spring/Summer 2027 Ready-to-Wear collection, The Remembering (Ncheta), which draws inspiration from the artistry of ancient Igbo-Ukwu bronze works. Its fitted silhouette is covered in painterly blue textures across the bodice and hips, while an exaggerated organza ruffle frames the neckline and reappears at the hem. The layered, feather-like finish gives the gown an almost sculptural quality, making it a particularly interesting interpretation of the collection’s inspiration.

Cardi B wears a sculptural blue mermaid gown from Nigerian fashion house Weiz Dhurm Franklyn’s Spring/Summer 2027 Ready-to-Wear collection, The Remembering (Ncheta), for her Billboard Canada editorial. Photo Credit: Weiz Dhurm Franklyn/Instagram 

Then comes Sevon Dejana, with a two-piece couture creation from the label’s Out of Body Haute Couture Spring/Summer 2027 collection. Cardi wears a structured, high-neck jacket with long sleeves and a matching skirt, both covered in intricate gold, red and wine-coloured crystals. Three-dimensional crimson floral details add another layer to the design, while a towering floral headpiece completes the look. Set against a lush botanical backdrop, the entire styling leans into the collection’s dramatic, otherworldly direction.

Cardi B wears a crystal-embroidered structured jacket and skirt from Nigerian designer Sevon Dejana’s Out of Body Haute Couture Spring/Summer 2027 collection for Billboard Canada. Photo Credit: Sevon Dejana/Instagram 

Of course, there’s more to Cardi’s Billboard Canada cover story than the fashion. The Grammy-winning rapper also gets candid about life as a mother of four, working through self-doubt and making history with her sold-out Little Miss Drama arena tour across North America. Looking back on a year that has included the release of her chart-topping second album, Am I the Drama?, and new business ventures, she tells the magazine that the past twelve months have reminded her of who she is.

item.content:encoded:
Eghosa Imasuen, Managing Director of Narrative Landscape Press and Othuke Ominiabohs, Chief Executive Officer of Masobe Books

Two of Nigeria’s foremost independent publishers, Masobe Books and Narrative Landscape Press, have announced a collaboration to bring Narrative Landscape’s titles to the Masobe App. The partnership marks a significant milestone for African literature, bringing some of the continent’s most celebrated literary works to a single, dedicated reading platform.

Under the agreement, readers using the Masobe App, which was launched on 23rd March 2026, will soon be able to discover, purchase, and read titles from Narrative Landscape’s distinguished list alongside the existing Masobe Books catalogue. The integration brings together two complementary publishing houses whose lists have helped define contemporary Nigerian writing over the past decade, and represents one of the most ambitious cross-publisher digital initiatives in the African literary space to date.

The collaboration is announced to address some of the most persistent challenges facing African readers and writers: discoverability, affordability and accessibility. By consolidating two of the country’s most respected catalogues onto a single, locally built platform, the partnership ensures African readers at home and across the diaspora can access a richer, deeper library of homegrown stories without the friction of fragmented distribution channels.

“This collaboration is a statement of intent. African writing deserves world-class infrastructure, and by bringing Narrative Landscape’s exceptional catalogue onto the Masobe App, we are building exactly that. Together, we are creating a home where the best of our stories can live, be discovered, and be read,” said Othuke Ominiabohs, the Chief Executive Officer for Masobe Books.

Narrative Landscape Press’s Managing Director, Eghosa Imasuen, said, “We have long believed that the future of African publishing depends on collaboration, not competition. Partnering with Masobe Books to make our titles available on the Masobe App means our authors will reach more readers, on a platform built with African readers at its core. This is a proud moment for everyone who believes in the power of our stories.”

From the rollout date, Masobe App users can expect a phased introduction of Narrative Landscape titles spanning literary fiction, narrative non-fiction, romance, fantasy, contemporary fiction, among others. The expanded library will include works from a roster of acclaimed authors who have shaped the recent literary landscape in Nigeria and beyond, including Chimamanda Ngozi Adichie, Chimeka Garricks, Yejide Kilanko, Abubakar Adam Ibrahim, Chibundo Onuzo and Fatima Bala.

The Masobe App, available on iOS and Android, has rapidly established itself as a leading destination for African literature, offering features tailored to local readers, including ebook, paperback and audiobook access; flexible payment options; reading goals and streaks; social networking, curated reading lists, and seamless mobile access. The addition of Narrative Landscape’s catalogue significantly deepens the platform’s offering and reinforces its position as a central hub for African stories.

item.dc:creator: BellaNaija.com
item.description:
Veteran Nollywood actor and retired broadcaster Chief Dr Pete Edochie, MON, passed away at 79 on Wednesday, 25 November 2026, in Enugu after a battle with prostate cancer.

The post Nollywood Legend Pete Edochie Passes Away at 79 appeared first on BellaNaija - Showcasing Africa to the world. Read today!.
item.content:encoded:
Nollywood icon Pete Edochie, MON, who passed away at the age of 79 in Enugu. Photo Credit: Pete Edochie/Instagram 

Nollywood and the wider African entertainment community are mourning the loss of one of their most respected screen icons, Pete Edochie, MON, who passed away on Wednesday, 25 November 2026,at the age of 79.

According to an official statement released on behalf of the family by his eldest son, Leo Pete Edochie, the veteran actor and retired broadcaster departed this life at 12:30 a.m. in Enugu, Nigeria, following a protracted battle with prostate cancer.

Born on 7 March 1947 in Zaria, Kaduna State, and hailing from Akamnato, Ifite Nteje in Anambra State, Pete Edochie began his career in broadcasting long before becoming a household name on television and cinema screens. At age 20, in 1967, he joined the Eastern Nigeria Broadcasting Service (ENBS)—later the Anambra Broadcasting Service (ABS)—rising steadily through the ranks to serve as Director of Programmes and Deputy Managing Director.

His defining breakthrough came in 1987 when he portrayed the fierce, tragic hero Okonkwo in the Nigerian Television Authority’s (NTA) acclaimed television adaptation of Chinua Achebe‘s Things Fall Apart. His commanding presence and deep, resonant voice earned him international recognition—including a dedicated delegation interview from the BBC—and cemented his place in Nigerian television history.

Over a screen career spanning nearly four decades, Pete Edochie became synonymous with authority,traditional wisdom, and unforgettable Igbo proverbs. Whether playing stern monarchs, principled elders, or complex patriarchs, he delivered every line with unmistakable gravitas. His extensive filmography includes standout appearances in classics and modern hits alike, such as Things Fall Apart (1987), Igodo (1999), Egg of Life (2003), Oracle (2003), Billionaires Club (2003), End of Money (2005), Lionheart (2018)—where he starred as Chief Ernest Obiagu alongside Genevieve Nnaji—Unroyal (2020), and Foreigner’s God (2022).

In recognition of his immense contributions to Nigerian arts and culture, he was conferred with the national honour of Member of the Order of the Niger (MON) in 2003 by former President Olusegun Obasanjo,alongside the Africa Magic Viewers’ Choice Awards (AMVCA) Industry Merit Award and lifetime achievement honours from the Africa Film Academy and the African Film Festival (TAFF).

Veteran Nollywood actor Chief Dr Pete Edochie and his wife, Barrister Mrs Josephine Edochie, at a church service. Photo Credit: Pete Edochie/Instagram 

Chief Dr Pete Edochie is survived by his beloved wife of over five decades, Barrister Mrs Josephine Edochie, their six children—Leo, Adam, Linc, Jean, Yul, and Eva Edochie (with Linc and Yul following closely in his acting footsteps)—as well as his siblings, grandchildren, and extended family.

Read the full statement from the Edochie family below:

Dear Friends, Colleagues, Business Associates and Well Wishers of Chief Dr Pete Edochie (M.O.N)

AN IROKO HAS FALLEN

With profound sadness and hearts bowed in total submission to the will of Almighty God, we announce the passing of our beloved husband, father, brother and kinsman, Chief Dr Pete EDOCHIE, MON (Ononenyi), a retired broadcaster and veteran Actor, who departed this life on Wednesday, 25th November 2026 at 12.30am after a protracted battle with prostate cancer in Enugu, Nigeria. He was aged 79 years.

Chief Dr Pete EDOCHIE hailed from Akamnato Ifite Nteje and is survived by his beloved wife, Barrister Mrs Josephine Edochie, his children, siblings and numerous other relations.

Funeral arrangements will be announced in due course.

As we mourn this painful loss, we pray that Almighty God grants his gentle soul eternal rest and gives the entire family the fortitude to bear this irreparable loss.

May God be with us all at this trying time.

Amen

Chief Leo Pete EDOCHIE

For the Family

item.content:encoded:
Falz and Simi reunite on their new single “Jaiye”, ten years after their 2016 joint EP Chemistry. Photo Credit: Falz/Instagram

Your playlist called, it wants a proper refresh before the week runs away from you. Between surprise link-ups from two of Afrobeats’ biggest names, cheeky big-money banter, and easy-going tunes built for the dance floor, Nigerian artists have given us plenty to queue up right now.

If you are hunting for something smooth to soundtrack your Lagos traffic commute, gearing up for a night out, or simply tired of hitting replay on the same ten tracks, here are five new Nigerian songs to listen to this week that deserve a spot in your rotation.

Rema featuring Wizkid – “Feel Alright”

When Rema and Wizkid finally lock into the studio together, you press play immediately. Serving as the opening track on Rema’s freshly released seven-track EP, E-Mortal Boy (EMB)—which follows his 2024 album HEIS and 2023’s Ravage EP—”Feel Alright” brings two generations of global Afrobeats stars onto one mid-tempo groove. Rema glides across the beat in a mix of English, Pidgin, and Yoruba while pursuing a love interest, before Wizkid slides in with his laid-back cadence. The official lyric video is already out too, so you can catch every bar from start to finish.

Adekunle Gold featuring Blaqbonez – “Money in a Wheelbarrow”

Did you ever picture Adekunle Gold and Blaqbonez on the same track? Adekunle Gold revealed that this single actually reunites him with an artist who dropped a diss track about him years ago—and marks their second attempt at making a song together. Arriving after Adekunle Gold’s Fuji album era and Blaqbonez’s fifth studio album, NOMADINHO: 4TH PRIME, “Money in a Wheelbarrow” turns big-money talk into a two-and-a-half-minute celebration of hard-earned wins. Adekunle Gold brings warm, melodic ease to the hook while Blaqbonez trades witty verses about stacking cash and enjoying the fruits of your grind right now.

Falz featuring Simi – “Jaiye”

Ten years after their beloved 2016 joint EP, Chemistry—and following favourites like “Soldier” and their 2024 duet “Borrow Me Your Baby” from Simi’s Lost and Found album—Falz and Simi are back together on “Jaiye“. Following Falz’s 2024 EP Before The Feast and his 2026 project Break Time, this new single leans into bright, feel-good rhythms and relatable Nigerian humour about choosing enjoyment despite the daily hustle. Falz brings his witty, conversational flow while Simi answers with silky vocals that remind you why fans never get tired of hearing them side by side.

Olamide featuring FOLA – “Jaiye”

Fresh off the release of his 10-track studio album, Time and Space—which arrived on 16 November following the lead single “Burukutu”, his 2025 self-titled album Olamidé, and his 2024 EP Ikigai Vol. 1—Olamide teams up with rising star FOLA for the project’s sole guest appearance on “Jaiye”. Sitting at track seven on the self-painted album, the collaboration pairs FOLA’s emotive, melodic vocals with Olamide’s grounded street delivery, giving you a soulful record about enjoying life that stays with you long after the first spin.

Joeboy – “Pretty Girls”

Taken from his five-track Lavida Boy EP—which follows his 2025 album Viva Lavida and 2023’s Body & Soul—Joeboy serves up a sweet, dance-ready tribute to confident women who love having a good time. Inspired by the classic Diwali riddim, “Pretty Girls” rides on lively percussion and an easy, sing-along hook that pulls you straight toward the dance floor.

item.title: Senegal Reinstated as 2025 AFCON Champions After Winning CAS Appeal
item.dc:creator: BellaNaija.com
item.description:
Senegal have been reinstated as 2025 AFCON champions after the Court of Arbitration for Sport overturned CAF's ruling and upheld their 1–0 win over Morocco.

The post Senegal Reinstated as 2025 AFCON Champions After Winning CAS Appeal appeared first on BellaNaija - Showcasing Africa to the world. Read today!.
item.content:encoded:
Idrissa Gana Gueye and captain Sadio Mané hold the 2025 Africa Cup of Nations trophy, which the Court of Arbitration for Sport confirmed belongs to Senegal after setting aside CAF’s Appeal Board decision.

The months-long off-pitch dispute surrounding the 2025 Africa Cup of Nations (AFCON) final has come to an official close, with Senegal reinstated as the tournament’s champions.

Today, Tuesday, 24 November 2026, the Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS)—the independent international body headquartered in Lausanne, Switzerland, that settles global sports disputes through arbitration—ruled unanimously in favour of the Senegalese Football Federation (FSF). The verdict overturns the Confederation of African Football (CAF) Appeal Board’s earlier decision that stripped the Teranga Lions of the trophy and handed a 3–0 forfeit victory to hosts Morocco.

For football lovers across the continent, many of whom watched two of Africa’s finest sides battle through one of the most dramatic finals in AFCON history, the verdict restores the outcome decided on the pitch in Rabat on 18 January 2026.

In that January final at the Prince Moulay Abdellah Stadium, Senegal edged Morocco 1–0 after extra time courtesy of a decisive strike from Pape Gueye. However, the match had been halted late in regulation time while still goalless after referee Jean–Jacques Ngambo Ndala awarded Morocco a penalty following a VAR review. Several Senegalese players walked off the pitch in protest for roughly 14 minutes before returning—following interventions from teammates including captain Sadio Mané—to finish the match in the 109th minute (90+19). Morocco’s Brahim Díaz missed the resulting penalty, and Senegal went on to win in extra time.

Senegal celebrate their 2025 Africa Cup of Nations triumph in Rabat—a title officially restored on 24 November 2026 after the Court of Arbitration for Sport overturned CAF’s forfeiture ruling.

Two months later, in March 2026, CAF’s Appeal Board ruled that Senegal’s temporary walk-off amounted to a forfeiture under Articles 82 and 84 of the competition regulations, awarding Morocco a 3–0 administrative win and the championship.

The FSF lodged its appeal with CAS on 25 March 2026, followed by a closed-door hearing in Lausanne on 8 October 2026 before a three-member panel presided over by French sports law expert Prof. Gérald Simon, alongside Prof. Luigi Fumagalli (Italy) and Prof. Dr. Ulrich Haas (Germany).

In its official statement released today, CAS confirmed that Senegal’s original victory stands: “The Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS) has upheld the appeal by the Senegalese Football Federation (FSF) against the Confederation of African Football (CAF) and the Royal Moroccan Football Federation (FRMF, in French) concerning the final of the Africa Cup of Nations Morocco 2025 (AFCON 2025). The decision rendered by the CAF Appeal Board is set aside and the decision by the CAF Disciplinary Board is reinstated. Consequently, the result obtained at the end of the AFCON 2025 final is confirmed (1-0 for Senegal).”

Explaining its reasoning, the panel noted that the referee’s decision to restart play fell squarely within his sole authority and was protected by football’s “field of play” doctrine, meaning it could not be overturned retrospectively.

“By blowing his whistle to restart play, the Referee considered that the conditions for resuming the match had been met – both teams were on the pitch again, and both expressed their willingness to resume,” CAS stated. “In the Panel’s view, there is no doubt that the effects of the Referee’s decision were limited to the pitch. As such, the Panel considers that the Referee’s decision was covered by the ‘field of play’ doctrine.”

Senegal captain Sadio Mané celebrates on his teammates’ shoulders with the 2025 AFCON trophy, officially restored to the Teranga Lions after CAS ruled in favour of the Senegalese Football Federation.

The panel also rejected arguments from the Royal Moroccan Football Federation (FRMF) that the referee had acted arbitrarily or erred in law, adding that Articles 82 and 84 of the AFCON regulations apply only when a match is permanently abandoned—not when play resumes and concludes. “The Panel acknowledged that the Referee had to make a decision in an atmosphere of extreme tension,” the statement added. “However, these circumstances do not justify describing the decision as ‘arbitrary’. On the contrary, the Referee’s judgment did not appear to have been affected by factors external to the game.”

CAS further noted that separate disciplinary sanctions had already been handed down by CAF to the FSF, head coach Pape Thiaw, and certain players over the walk-off incident.

With the ruling now official, Senegal retain their second AFCON title, bringing a decisive close to one of the biggest off-pitch sagas in modern African football.

***

item.content:encoded:
Olam Agri’s wheat milling and pasta business, Crown Flour Mill (CFM) Limited, honoured its top customers, dealers and distributors at its Customer Awards & Recognition Night, marking more than 15 years of partnership.

Held under the theme “Celebrating Partnerships, Rewarding Excellence,” the event brought together company leadership and long-standing partners from Northern, Eastern and Western Nigeria. It paid tribute to the distributors who built markets and the dealers who remained committed through shifting economic conditions. Their enterprise and confidence have carried CFM’s products to customers and communities across the country.

The highlight of the evening was the rewarding of CFM’s best-performing dealers across three categories: Trailblazer, Sterling and Titan. Winners received 5-tonne, 10-tonne and 15-tonne trucks, as well as baking ovens. The night closed with the presentation of a 45-tonne truck to the overall best-performing dealer.

L-R: Charles Babarimisa, Head of Sales; Siddharth Suri, Vice President/Business Head; Nitin Mehta, Managing Director, all of Crown Flour Mill (CFM) Limited; and Alhaji Oluwasesan Sose, the overall best-performing distributor and winner of a 45-tonne truck, during the presentation of award prizes.

Nitin Mehta, Business Head, Wheat Milling & Pasta Business, Olam Agri, said the milestone reflects far more than time.

“Fifteen years of growing together represents relationships built on trust, shared ambition and resilience. Our dealers and distributors have helped us extend our market reach, serve customers better and strengthen our position in the industry. Through changing market dynamics and different challenges, the strength of our partnerships has been a constant source of resilience.”

Sanusi Modinat (5th from right), a dealer, with her award and the key to a 15-tonne truck, her reward for her performance.

Bolaji Anifowose, Vice President & Commercial, Olam Agri, described dealers as strategic partners rather than an extension of the distribution network.

“Their market knowledge, entrepreneurial drive and commitment connect our brands to consumers across the country. Our focus now is on strengthening these partnerships, improving market reach, enhancing distribution efficiency and creating more opportunities for our partners to grow. A stronger dealer network means a stronger business.”

 

The overall best-performing dealer, Alhaji Oluwaseun Sose, called the award a proud moment.

“My relationship with the company has been built on trust, consistency and a shared commitment to growth. It has been a journey of learning, overcoming challenges and identifying opportunities together. This recognition encourages me to keep striving for excellence.”

The runner-up, Opeyemi Sanusi Modinat, praised the company’s collaborative approach.

“Our partnership has given us opportunities to grow, expand our market presence and serve more customers. What makes it special is the understanding that our success matters too.”

Anil Nair, Managing Director and Country Head, Olam Agri Nigeria, said the evening reflected the company’s enduring commitment to its partners.

“Our dealers and distributors are an integral part of our business, our growth and our connection with consumers. Their resilience and belief in our business have helped us navigate different market realities and seize opportunities together. Our success is strongest when our partners succeed.”

Olam Agri will continue to deepen its relationships with customers and distribution partners, strengthen its market presence and create new opportunities for shared growth. It will do so through improved partner engagement, business development support and initiatives that boost dealers’ competitiveness.

About Olam Agri

Olam Agri is a market-leading, differentiated food, feed and fibre agri-business with a global origination footprint, processing capabilities and a deep understanding of market needs built over 37 years. With a strong presence in high-growth emerging markets, it offers products across grains & oilseeds, wheat milling & pasta, rice, edible oils, animal feed & protein, cotton, wood products, rubber, sugar & biofuel, freight management and risk management solutions. We are at the heart of global food and agri-trade flows, providing affordable food staples and processed agricultural products that are daily necessities and living essentials for people around the world.

Driven by our Purpose to transform food, feed and fibre for a more sustainable and food-secure future, we aim to create value for customers and enable farming communities to prosper sustainably. Olam Agri is majority-owned (81.81%) by the Saudi Agricultural and Livestock Investment Company (SALIC) and is an associated company of Olam Group, which owns 18.19%. Led by WISCAR Founder and Chairperson, Amina Oyagbola, the walk forms part of the lead-up to the organisation’s 18th Annual Leadership and Mentoring Conference.

Participants were paired up for the walk along the Eko Atlantic, each with someone they had not met before. At the end of the route, they switched to new mentor-mentee partners for a short mentoring session, which gave everyone two fresh conversations in one morning.
Back at the meeting point, participants shared what they had learnt from their partners, from career advice to personal lessons.

Nutritionist Sherese Ijewere then led a session on healthy eating and answered questions on everyday food choices. Coach Bobbie Tee of Happy Heart Fitness, closed the morning with a Zumba session.

Next stop: the conference

The walk sets the stage for WISCAR’s 18th Annual Leadership and Mentoring Conference, themed “Courage in Action: Shaping Policies and Structures for Inclusive Progress.” The conference takes place on Saturday, November 28, 2026, at the Civic Centre, Lagos.

Highlights include:

  • A keynote from Dr Ndidi Nwuneli, former President and CEO of the ONE Campaign and Founder of LEAP Africa, who will also receive this year’s Distinguished WISCAR Award.
  • Speakers including  Badejo-Okusanya, SAN, President of the Nigerian Bar Association, and Mallam Ahmed Ladan Gobir, President of the Chartered Institute of Personnel Management (CIPM)
  • The launch of WISCAR’s CIPM-endorsed Corporate Mentoring Playbook
