item.content:encoded:
Have you ever spent six hours in an airport waiting for your connecting flight, watching the departure screens, browsing duty-free shops and wondering what the city outside looks like? Perhaps you were connecting through Istanbul, Doha, Dubai or Addis Ababa. You were technically in another country, but the closest you came to experiencing it was buying a souvenir at the airport.

What if I told you that some airlines could help you turn that connection into an additional holiday, sometimes even providing accommodation? Having travelled to more than 70 countries, I have learnt that one of the smartest ways to travel is to pay attention to the journey, not just the destination. Many Nigerians book international tickets based on price, travel time and baggage allowance. These are important considerations, but there is another question worth asking: What else can this ticket give me?

I am talking about stopovers, not the hurried two-hour connection where you are running between terminals, but an intentional break in your journey that allows you to experience another destination before continuing to the country you originally planned to visit. And with the right airline, itinerary and travel documents, that additional experience might cost less than you imagine.

First, Understand What You Are Booking

A layover is generally a connection between flights; a stopover is a longer, planned break in your journey. Airlines define these differently, and the distinction matters because some offer special hotel packages, sightseeing tours or complimentary accommodation to qualifying passengers.

For example, imagine travelling from Lagos to London through Istanbul. Instead of spending a few hours at Istanbul Airport, you could investigate whether your ticket qualifies for a longer stopover, allowing you to explore Istanbul before continuing to London. You have now turned one international journey into an opportunity to experience two destinations outside Nigeria. The secret is to investigate the stopover before purchasing your ticket, rather than arriving at the airport and hoping the airline will allow you to stay longer.

Turkish Airlines: Turn Istanbul Into Part of Your Holiday

Turkish Airlines operates a Stopover in Istanbul programme for eligible international passengers connecting through Istanbul Airport. For visa purposes, Nigerians do not qualify, but with a valid Turkish visa you would be able to qualify for some of the perks. 

Qualifying travellers with connections of at least 20 hours and up to seven days may receive complimentary hotel accommodation. Under the standard programme, eligible Economy Class passengers can receive one night in a four-star hotel, while Business Class passengers may receive two nights in a five-star or boutique hotel.

Imagine travelling from Abuja or Lagos through Istanbul to London, Paris or another European destination. Rather than treating Istanbul as somewhere you simply change planes, you could plan time to experience the Grand Bazaar, the Bosphorus and the city’s extraordinary cultural heritage. The programme has specific conditions, including qualifying return tickets, participating countries of departure and an application made at least 72 hours before the relevant flight.

The complimentary accommodation does not cover every expense. Airport transfers, visa fees and other personal costs remain your responsibility. And for Nigerian passport holders, permission to enter Türkiye must be established before departure. A hotel voucher is not a substitute for a visa. There is also Touristanbul, a separate complimentary sightseeing programme for eligible passengers with shorter connections, typically between six and 24 hours. The two programmes have different conditions and cannot simply be combined.

Qatar Airways: A Stopover That Requires More Planning

Qatar Airways offers an opportunity to turn a connection through Doha into an additional holiday. However, for Nigerian passport holders, there is an important distinction between the airline’s advertised stopover offers and the actual requirements for entering Qatar.

While Qatar Airways promotes discounted stopover accommodation, Nigerian travellers should not assume they can access these packages without first satisfying Qatar’s visa requirements. Under the arrangement applicable to Nigerian travellers, obtaining the relevant visa requires purchasing an eligible Discover Qatar package with a minimum of three nights’ accommodation from accredited travel companies in Nigeria.

This means the stopover is not necessarily an opportunity to enjoy complimentary or heavily discounted accommodation. Instead, its value lies in the possibility of incorporating Doha into an international journey without purchasing an entirely separate return flight from Nigeria. For example, if you are travelling from Lagos to Singapore through Doha, you could investigate a ticket that allows you to spend three nights in Qatar before continuing to Singapore.

You would still need to budget for the qualifying Discover Qatar accommodation package, visa requirements, meals, activities and other expenses. The potential saving is therefore in the flight arrangement rather than the hotel. This is an important lesson about stopover programmes: what an airline advertises globally may not be equally accessible to every passport holder. Before booking, confirm your visa eligibility, the required Discover Qatar package and whether the extended stopover changes your airfare.

Ethiopian Airlines: Discover Addis Ababa on Your Way to Another Destination

For travellers heading to destinations across Africa and beyond, Ethiopian Airlines offers an opportunity worth investigating.

Eligible passengers connecting through Addis Ababa for between eight and 24 hours on qualifying Ethiopian Airlines tickets can receive complimentary hotel accommodation, meals and airport transfers. The airline also offers sightseeing experiences through Ethiopian Holidays.

Imagine flying from Abuja to Cape Town through Addis Ababa. Instead of spending a long connection inside the airport, you could use an eligible stopover to experience Ethiopian coffee culture, local cuisine and some of the capital’s attractions before continuing to South Africa.

The airline generally issues accommodation vouchers to qualifying passengers at their departure airport or transit desk (but make sure you already have your visa before going to the desk).

Passengers wishing to leave the airport must still satisfy Ethiopia’s entry requirements. The airline may assist with transit documentation under its qualifying programme, but this should be confirmed before travel. For me, this is an excellent example of how a journey through Africa can become an opportunity to discover more of the continent.

Emirates: Understand the Difference Between Dubai Connect and a Dubai Holiday

Dubai is already a familiar destination to many Nigerian travellers, but there is an important distinction between deliberately stopping in Dubai and qualifying for Emirates’ Dubai Connect service.

Dubai Connect can provide accommodation and other transit assistance to eligible passengers with qualifying connections, generally between six and 26 hours. However, it is designed around the best available flight connection, not simply a passenger’s desire to extend a holiday.

If you deliberately choose a much longer connection when a shorter eligible one exists, you may not qualify for the complimentary service. That does not mean you cannot plan Dubai into a wider holiday. You can investigate a paid multi-city itinerary or a ticket that allows a longer stay. UAE government is also constantly changing its rules, so make sure to check all this properly before booking that trip.

For example, you might arrange Lagos to Dubai, spend several nights there, then continue to Bangkok or Singapore before returning home. But that is a planned multi-city journey, not necessarily a free airline stopover. Understanding the difference prevents disappointment and unexpected expenses.

EgyptAir and Royal Air Maroc: Look Beyond the Obvious Hubs

Two other airlines worth investigating are EgyptAir and Royal Air Maroc.

EgyptAir provides transit accommodation in Cairo for certain qualifying international connections. Depending on the cabin, fare and connection, the minimum transit period may be six or eight hours, with accommodation generally limited to eligible connections of no more than 24 hours. It is also important that you either get the ‘ok to board’, which allows you to qualify for a visa on arrival from an accredited agent, or you can qualify for a visa on arrival with a UK, US, Schengen, or Canadian visa.

A traveller flying through Cairo could therefore investigate whether a qualifying connection provides an opportunity to experience Egypt before continuing to Europe or another destination.

Royal Air Maroc also provides transit assistance in Casablanca, including meals and, in certain circumstances, hotel accommodation subject to availability. For travellers connecting through Morocco to Europe, Casablanca could become more than an airport on the way to somewhere else. This is most possible for those with Morocco visas from the embassy in Abuja or those who qualify for E-visas (UK, US,Schengen,Canada etc visa).

However, neither airline’s transit accommodation policy should be mistaken for an unrestricted complimentary holiday. The rules depend on the ticket, connection and immigration requirements.

How to Actually Book a Stopover

Before purchasing your next international ticket, I suggest following a simple process.

First, identify the airline’s connecting hub. If you are flying Turkish Airlines, investigate Istanbul. If you are flying Qatar Airways, look at Doha. For Ethiopian Airlines, consider Addis Ababa.

Second, visit the airline’s official website and search for its stopover programme. Do not assume that selecting a long connection automatically qualifies you for complimentary accommodation.

Third, compare the ordinary return fare with an eligible stopover or multi-city itinerary. Check whether changing the connection increases the ticket price.

Fourth, confirm what the airline actually provides. Some programmes include a hotel and meals. Others offer discounted accommodation. Some provide tours, while others only assist with overnight transit.

Finally, check your visa eligibility before making any nonrefundable payments, and most importantly, if you’re not sure, speak to an IATA-accredited travel agent to guide you.

This final point is particularly important for Nigerian passport holders. A country may allow you to transit through its airport without a visa but require separate permission before you can leave the terminal.

The Real Savings Are in the Planning

Let us be clear: adding another destination is not automatically free. Even when an airline provides complimentary accommodation, you may still need to pay for visas, meals, transport and activities.

But compare that with purchasing an entirely separate international return ticket from Nigeria to visit the same country another time. You may find that a carefully planned stopover provides better overall value.

There is also the question of time. A 20-hour stopover does not mean 20 hours of sightseeing. Immigration, airport transfers, hotel check-in, and your next departure all reduce the time available. Sometimes a short guided tour is the sensible choice. Sometimes a full night or two allows you to enjoy the city properly.

And sometimes, the fastest connection is still the best option. The objective is not to complicate every journey. It is to understand the opportunities available before deciding.

Before You Book Your Next Flight

As we approach another year of travel, I want you to look differently at the international tickets you are considering. If you are travelling through Istanbul, Doha, Addis Ababa, Dubai, Cairo or Casablanca, ask what opportunities exist beyond the departure lounge.

Check the airline’s stopover conditions. Investigate its hotel arrangements. Compare the cost of extending your journey. And, most importantly, make sure you have the correct travel documents. You may discover that the airline taking you to your holiday destination can also introduce you to somewhere completely different.

Because sometimes, travelling more is not about buying another ticket; it is about discovering how much more you can do with the journey you are already taking.

item.content:encoded:
Chef Soliat Bada

Anyone who grew up in a Nigerian home knows the line. You suggest buying food outside, and before you finish the sentence, someone reminds you that there’s rice at home. It is usually the end of the conversation. In Asali Africa’s new series, it is where the conversation starts.

There’s Rice at Home is a cooking and conversation show from Asali Africa, the Lagos-based creative development agency, hosted by Chef Soliat Bada. In each episode, Soliat cooks one rice dish with a guest, and while the pot does its work, the two get into the kind of talk that usually happens around food: family, money and what success really looks like.

Rice is the most ordinary thing in a Nigerian kitchen, and the show makes a good case that it doesn’t have to taste ordinary. Over five episodes, released every two weeks, the menu travels from Jamaica to Saudi Arabia, back home to Nigeria and on to Louisiana.

You don’t just watch the food get made, either. The recipes are written up in full on Asali Africa’s website, with the ingredients and method laid out step by step, so you can watch Soliat cook a dish and then make it in your own kitchen.

The season opens with Rice and Peas with Oxtail, the Jamaican Sunday staple of rice cooked in coconut milk with red kidney beans (the “peas”), served beside rich, slow-cooked oxtail. Soliat’s guest is Michael Famoroti, co-founder of Stears, and their conversation turns to family and black tax: the expectation that once you start earning, you start supporting the people who raised you. Read the full recipe for Rice and Peas with Oxtail.

Rice and peas with oxtail, from Episode 1

Soliat Bada and Michael Famoroti in Episode 1

Episode 2 moves to the Gulf for lamb kabsa, Saudi Arabia’s national dish, fragrant with dried lime and seven spice. Soliat is joined by Bella Adeleke, CEO of Asali Africa and founder of the fashion label Garbe, for a conversation about redefining success. Read the full recipe for Lamb Kabsa.

Lamb kabsa, from Episode 2

Still to come are Nigerian fried rice with fried turkey and dodo, cooked with Toyin Jolapamo and Nneoma Mere; jambalaya with Goldie Iyamu and Vanessa Iloenyosi; and a season finale with Edwin Okolo and Temi Omolehinwa.

For more on Asali Africa and the products and ideas it develops, visit asali.africa.

item.content:encoded:
The presence of Mini LED tells a shopper something important about the light source behind an LCD panel.
It does not, by itself, explain how that light is arranged, divided or controlled. Those implementation choices can have a major influence on contrast, black level performance, highlight control and the visibility of blooming in difficult scenes.

From Presence To Performance

That distinction matters because a category becomes more useful to consumers when it can be evaluated through clear performance principles rather than through a technology name alone. For Mini LED, three factors provide a practical starting point.

The first is hardware local dimming. In a hardware based system, physical groups of LEDs can be brightened, dimmed or switched off independently across different areas of the screen. This gives the television more direct control over how light is distributed within a single image.

The second is local dimming zone count and precision. A higher number of independently controlled zones can allow the backlight to respond in smaller areas, which can improve separation between bright highlights and surrounding dark regions when other major conditions are comparable. The number itself is not the whole story, but it is a useful indicator of how granular the backlight system can be.

The third is backlight architecture. Full Array Local Dimming places controllable zones across the area behind the panel, providing the physical foundation for more localized light management than designs that illuminate the panel from the edges or operate the backlight more uniformly.

Together, these three elements move the Mini LED conversation from a simple question of whether the technology is present to a more useful question: how effectively is the light being controlled?

 Where TCL Enters The Category Conversation

TCL is relevant to that discussion because Mini LED has become a significant part of its global television business. According to Omdia data cited in TCL Electronics interim results, TCL ranked No. 1 globally by Mini LED TV shipment volume in the first half of 2026. TCL reported 2.43 million Mini LED TV shipments during the period, representing 77.1% year on year growth.

That position follows a strong 2025, when TCL reported, based on Omdia data, a 31.1% share of global Mini LED TV shipments and 118.0% year on year shipment growth.

Market scale does not, on its own, define technology leadership. What it does provide is evidence that a manufacturer has become an important participant in how the category develops. For a company operating at that scale, leadership increasingly includes helping make the technology easier to understand and giving consumers clearer ways to evaluate what they are buying.

Defining Category Leadership

Category leadership in Mini LED should therefore be broader than shipment rankings. It can be understood through four connected areas: sustained market scale, continued investment in the fundamentals of backlight performance, clearer performance criteria, and education that helps consumers distinguish between different implementations of the technology.

This is where the idea of good Mini LED becomes useful. It does not require creating a new certification or suggesting that every television should perform identically. It simply encourages a more complete discussion of the hardware and architecture that sit behind the Mini LED name.

Source references for internal verification:

  • • Omdia, Global TV shipments grow 3.6% in 2Q26 as market headwinds intensify, August 2026. Mini LED accounted for 13% of global TV shipments in Q2 2026.
  • • TCL Electronics 2026 Interim Results, citing Omdia global brand Mini LED TV shipment data for H1 2026. TCL reported 2.43 million Mini LED TV shipments, up 77.1% year on year, with shipment volume ranked No. 1 globally.
  • • TCL Electronics 2025 Annual Results, citing Omdia. TCL reported a 31.1% global Mini LED TV shipment share in 2025, ranked No. 1 globally, with shipments up 118.0% year on year.

item.content:encoded:
The third edition of the Lagos International Theatre Festival (LITF) has concluded successfully, attracting over 20,000 attendees from November 9 to 15, 2026. Featuring more than 25 productions, international performances from Kenya, Brazil, Norway and Canada, high-profile diplomatic engagements and a spectacular Opening Night Gala, the festival reinforced its growing position as an important platform for showcasing Nigerian creativity and connecting global theatre communities.
The impressive turnout, diversity of productions and international participation demonstrated the growing appetite for live theatre and the potential of cultural platforms to stimulate creative enterprise, encourage international collaboration and strengthen Nigeria’s global cultural presence.

A Vision For Global Recognition

Speaking on the success of the festival, Founder and Creative Producer, Bolanle Austen-Peters, said:

“Our ambition has always been to create more than a theatre festival. We want to build a platform that places Lagos firmly on the global cultural map, gives African stories the international visibility they deserve and creates meaningful opportunities for our artists. Welcoming over 20,000 attendees, presenting more than 25 productions and bringing international performers from four countries to Lagos is a powerful affirmation of this vision. Theatre is not just entertainment; it is an instrument of cultural identity, economic opportunity and global influence. The Stage Is Everywhere, and Africa must claim its rightful place on that stage.”

A Week Of Culture And Collaboration

The festival opened on November 9 with Theatre Meets Food at Kaly Restaurant, featuring celebrated chef Hilda Baci in a unique fusion of culinary artistry and live performance. The week also featured diplomatic and cultural engagements hosted by the United States Consul General in Lagos and the British Embassy, alongside a networking reception organised by the British Council for festival directors and participating production companies. These engagements highlighted the importance of international partnerships and cultural diplomacy in advancing Nigeria’s creative industry.

A Celebration Of Excellence

A major highlight was the Opening Night Gala, held on November 13 at Shell Hall, MUSON Centre, which welcomed over 1,000 guests, including the Governor of Lagos State, Babajide Olusola Sanwo-Olu; the Chargé d’Affaires of the US Mission in Nigeria; the US Consul General; the British Deputy High Commissioner; the Consul General of Brazil; the Consul General of South Africa, the Ambassador of the Republic of Korea; alongside other members of the diplomatic corps, heads of institutions, government representatives, international delegates and leading figures in the creative industry.

The Governor received an award in recognition of his support for the arts, while renowned theatre practitioner Ben Tomoloju received a Lifetime Achievement and Legacy Award for his enduring contributions to the development of the arts in Nigeria.

A Global Stage For Theatre

The festival’s main performance programme took place from November 14 to 15 across MUSON Centre, Ouida and KAP Hub, featuring over 25 productions spanning established and emerging Nigerian creatives, school and children’s performances, and international works.

The programme offered audiences diverse theatrical experiences while creating opportunities for cultural exchange and collaboration among Nigerian and international artists. Food, beverage and lifestyle brands also contributed to the festival atmosphere, extending the experience beyond the stage.

Reflecting on the achievement, Vanessa Jev, Festival Director, said:

“This year’s festival demonstrated what is possible when artistic vision, strong partnerships and collective commitment come together. Welcoming over 20,000 attendees, presenting more than 25 productions and hosting international participants from four countries required months of planning and the dedication of an exceptional team. We are proud to have created a platform where Nigerian and international artists could share their work, connect with new audiences and build lasting relationships. This success provides a stronger foundation for expanding the festival’s reach and creating greater opportunities for the creative community.”

LITF 2026 gratefully acknowledges its sponsors: Afreximbank, Waltersmith, Pillar Oil, LEDCO, Prime Atlantic, Nigerian Bottling Company, MTN and Wema Bank, whose generous support contributed to the success of the festival.

The festival also appreciates its partners: United States Consulate, British Deputy High Commission, British Council, Amstel Malta, Kaly, Beat FM, Classic FM, Smooth FM, Avis, Channels TV, BellaNaija, Africa Movie Channel, My Lagos App, Cadbury and Pulse for their invaluable collaboration and support.


Looking Ahead

The successful conclusion of LITF 2026 marks another important milestone in the festival’s ambition to position Lagos as a leading destination for theatre and performing arts in Africa. With growing audience engagement, international participation and institutional partnerships, LITF remains committed to showcasing exceptional talent, promoting cultural exchange and building a sustainable global platform for African storytelling.

LITF 2026 — THE STAGE IS EVERYWHERE.

About LITF

The Lagos International Theatre Festival is an annual celebration of theatre, storytelling and artistic expression, bringing together local and international productions, performers and creative professionals. Through performances, cultural engagements and industry collaborations, LITF promotes artistic excellence, encourages cultural exchange and supports the growth of the performing arts industry, with a vision to position Lagos as a leading theatre destination in Africa.

item.content:encoded:
Rema releases his seven-track EP, E-Mortal Boy (EMB), featuring Wizkid, Theodora, BNYX, and Kah-Lo. Photo Credit: Rema/Instagram

For weeks, Rema has been teasing us with a new project—first came “TEA” and then “Oh No“, and if you have had those on repeat on your playlist, you now have the entire package with his seven-track EP, E-Mortal Boy (EMB). Ever since his self-titled debut EP in 2019, the Benin-born star has never been interested in staying boxed into one sound. Following his 2023 EP Ravage and his 2024 Grammy-nominated album HEIS, he uses this new seven-song collection to pull rhythms from across the Black diaspora into one bold, genre-hopping ride.

If you already had “TEA” on loop when its dancehall bounce, glossy pop, and techno twists took over the Nigerian timeline, or kept “Oh No” close for that percussion-heavy Rvssian groove about a lover’s mixed signals, they both sit right inside the full lineup alongside five more records. The biggest headline moment opens the project: “Feel Alright” pairs Rema with Wizkid for their very first official joint release, a smooth ballad about satisfying a lover’s appetite. From there, he switches gears across “Velvet“, where rumba drums meet slick guitar riffs as he vows to take on the world for someone special, and “TANZANIA“, a BNYX-assisted track with Bollywood score-inspired flair.

The rest of the EP keeps that same adventurous streak alive. On “SUGA“, Rema teams up with French Congolese singer Theodora for a rougher, grunge-leaning sound, before closing out on “Bang Bang” with longtime collaborator London and Nigerian dance music favourite Kah-Lo. Nearly a decade into his run, Rema still sounds completely locked in on what comes next, leaving you with seven quick tracks to drop straight into your weekend rotation.

item.title: Raye Tops the 2027 Grammy Nominations With 11 Including Album of the Year
item.dc:creator: BellaNaija.com
item.description:
Leading the 2027 Grammy nominations with 11 nods, Raye picks up Album of the Year for This Music May Contain Hope and Record and Song of the Year for "WHERE IS MY HUSBAND!" alongside her emotional online reaction.

The post Raye Tops the 2027 Grammy Nominations With 11 Including Album of the Year appeared first on BellaNaija - Showcasing Africa to the world. Read today!.
item.content:encoded:
Raye singing on stage with her band and backing vocalists. Photo Credit: Raye/Instagram 

When the 2027 Grammy nominations dropped earlier this week, one name sat right at the top of the entire board: Raye. Out of every artist in the running for the 69th Annual Grammy Awards, she has the highest Grammy nominations this year with 11 nods, putting her ahead of Rosalía on nine.

If you have been watching her rise over the past few years, seeing her command this much spotlight on music’s biggest stage feels well earned, especially for readers following global talent with Ghanaian roots through her mother’s side of the family. Her reaction online captured just how surreal the moment felt, writing on Instagram: “WHAT IS HAPPENING WHAT IS HAPPENING 11 GRAMMY NOMINATIONS INCLUDING ALBUM OF THE YEAR MY HEARTTTTT CANNOT EVEN FATHOM, MY HEARTTTTTTTT ” before following up with a simple “can’t stop crying .”

Raye at home with her parents following the 2027 Grammy nominations announcement. Photo Credit: Raye/Instagram 

In case you are still catching up on her story, Raye was born Rachel Keen in London to a Ghanaian-Swiss mother and an English father, and she has spent years building a reputation as a sharp songwriter, vocalist, and arranger who refuses to stay boxed into one sound.

Many listeners first got to know her through chart-topping collaborations and pop hooks before she parted ways with her former major label to release music independently, taking full creative control of her catalogue and storytelling. That independent leap paid off massively—her album This Music May Contain Hope topped the UK chart in March 2026 and won the 2026 Mercury Prize in October, turning her into one of the most talked-about voices in music.

Artwork for This Music May Contain Hope. Photo Credit: Raye/Instagram 

Her 11 nominations for 2027 stretch right across her artistry, from songwriting and performance to arrangement, visuals, and full-length projects. This Music May Contain Hope is competing in both Album of the Year and Best Pop Vocal Album, while her hit “WHERE IS MY HUSBAND!“—which reached UK No. 1 in January 2026—is up for Record of the Year, Song of the Year, and Best Pop Solo Performance.

She also earned nods for “Click Clack Symphony” alongside Hans Zimmer in Best Pop Duo/Group Performance, Best Arrangement, Instrumental and Vocals, and Best Music Video, plus “Life Boat” in Best Dance Pop Recording, “I Hate the Way I Look Today” in Best Traditional Pop Vocal Performance, and a Songwriter of the Year, Non-Classical nod.

Raye holding a number one award following a year of UK chart milestones, including “WHERE IS MY HUSBAND!” hitting No. 1 in January 2026 and This Music May Contain Hope topping the UK chart in March 2026. Photo Credit: Raye/Instagram 

This is not her first time on the Grammy radar, though it is easily her biggest moment yet. Before this sweep, Raye had four prior Grammy nominations—taking her career total to 15—including Best New Artist, Songwriter of the Year, Non-Classical, and Best Engineered Album, Non-Classical in 2025, plus Best Music Film in 2026 for Live at the Royal Albert Hall.

While the Recording Academy previously honoured her with the noncompetitive Harry Belafonte Best Song for Social Change Award for her songwriting on “Ice Cream Man“, she has never won a competitive Grammy. With 11 chances coming up at the 2027 ceremony on February 7, 2027, we will all be watching to see if she finally brings home her first competitive win—or a whole shelf of them.

item.description:
Five African destinations—Kenya, Rwanda, Mauritius, Ghana, and Côte d'Ivoire—give Nigerian travellers easy entry for a Christmas holiday, mixing wildlife safaris, beach escapes, city dining, and full itineraries.

The post A Safari, a Beach & Easy Entry? 5 African Spots for Your Christmas Holiday appeared first on BellaNaija - Showcasing Africa to the world. Read today!.
item.content:encoded:
Five African destinations Nigerian passport holders can visit visa-free or with visa on arrival this Christmas holiday. Image: AI-generated.

The group chat has the concerts, the dinners and the Detty December link-ups covered. But has anyone planned the getaway? Beyond the usual Lagos parties and end-of-year outings, there is a whole continent waiting to be explored, with sun-soaked beaches, wildlife safaris, exciting food scenes and cities with plenty of stories to tell.

You do not have to spend weeks navigating embassy appointments and visa applications to make it happen, either. Several African countries offer Nigerian passport holders visa-free entry or visas on arrival, making a festive-season escape much easier to plan. Whether you are travelling solo, gathering your friends, taking the family along or joining a curated travel group, here are five destinations worth considering for your Christmas holiday.

Kenya

Imagine spotting lions and giraffes against a city skyline before breakfast, then catching an evening flight or train straight to the coast for fresh seafood by the Indian Ocean. That contrast is what makes Kenya such a rewarding December escape. Nairobi gives you immediate access to wildlife at Nairobi National Park and the Giraffe Centre alongside lively restaurants and art spaces in Westlands and Karen, while longer itineraries open up classic game drives in the Maasai Mara, views of Mount Kilimanjaro in Amboseli, and warm beach days in Diani or Watamu. Nigerian citizens enjoy visa-free entry for short stays of up to 60 days without needing a paid eTA, leaving more room in your budget for safaris and coastal stays.

Rwanda

Not everyone wants their year-end holiday to feel like a non-stop sprint, and Rwanda is built for travellers who prefer scenery, clean air, and an unhurried pace. Days in Kigali easily revolve around specialty coffee shops, contemporary art at Inema Arts Center, and a sobering, essential visit to the Kigali Genocide Memorial before you head out into the countryside. From the capital, you can track chimpanzees and walk above the trees in Nyungwe Forest, go on wildlife drives in Akagera National Park, or spend quiet afternoons along the shores of Lake Kivu. With 30-day visa-free entry for Nigerian passport holders, getting there is straightforward from start to finish.

Mauritius

Sometimes a proper Christmas break calls for leaving mainland schedules behind altogether for turquoise lagoons, catamaran cruises, and mountain trails. In Mauritius, you can base yourself around Grand Baie in the north for boat trips to Île aux Cerfs and lively beachside dinners, or head south-west toward Le Morne Brabant for coastal hikes and water sports. Between beach days, the bustling Central Market in Port Louis, the lush trails of Black River Gorges National Park, and Casela Nature Parks keep a week-long itinerary full without ever feeling hectic. Nigerian travellers receive a free 14-day visa on arrival, though you will need to fill out Mauritius’s free All-in-One Travel Digital Form and Health Declaration Form online before boarding.

Ghana

Staying close to home does not mean settling for the same routine, especially when Accra turns into one of West Africa’s busiest festive hubs every December. You can spend mornings browsing contemporary art at Gallery 1957 and walking through historic Jamestown, afternoons unwinding at Labadi Beach or Kokrobite, and nights hopping between concerts and street-food spots. Whenever you are ready for a change of scenery, a road trip to Cape Coast and Elmina brings historic castles and the treetop canopy walkway at Kakum National Park within easy reach, while Aburi and Akosombo offer cooler hills and riverside views. Thanks to ECOWAS free movement, Nigerian passport holders enter Ghana visa-free for up to 90 days by air or road.

Côte d’Ivoire

For a West African holiday with a distinct francophone rhythm, Côte d’Ivoire pairs cosmopolitan city life with laid-back coastal escapes just a short flight from Nigeria. Abidjan greets visitors with lagoon views, leafy walking trails inside Banco National Park, and vibrant late-night dining in Zone 4 and Cocody where grilled fish and attiéké steal the show. A quick drive east takes you to Grand-Bassam for quiet beaches, craft markets, and historic architecture, while Assinie offers resort-style downtime further along the coast. Covered under ECOWAS visa-free access for up to 90 days, it is an easy switch-up when you want familiar regional warmth with a fresh cultural flavour.

item.title: From Tunde Kelani to Akinola Davies Jr., 5 Nollywood Directors You Should Know

item.description:
Tunde Kelani, Akinola Davies Jr., Kemi Adetiba, Daniel Etim Effiong, and Dammy Twitch represent five Nigerian film directors shaping Nollywood across classic adaptations, award-winning dramas, and box-office hits.

The post From Tunde Kelani to Akinola Davies Jr., 5 Nollywood Directors You Should Know appeared first on BellaNaija - Showcasing Africa to the world. Read today!.
item.content:encoded:
From music visuals to international festival stages and actor-turned-director debuts, Dammy Twitch, Akinola Davies Jr., and Daniel Etim Effiong represent different paths into Nollywood directing.

Think about the Nigerian films and series you have watched recently, the ones that kept you glued to your screen, had you talking about the storyline long after the credits rolled or recommending them to everyone you know. While the actors are often the faces you remember first, there is someone behind the camera whose creative choices help bring those stories to life: the director.

From interpreting the script and guiding actors to shaping how each scene looks, sounds and unfolds, directors influence almost every part of what ends up on screen. As Nollywood grows in ambition, production quality and global reach, the filmmakers steering these projects are becoming just as central to the industry’s story as the stars in front of the lens. Some have spent decades bringing Nigerian literature and history to the screen, while others are earning international acclaim or crossing over from music videos into feature films. Here are five Nollywood directors whose work is worth knowing.

Tunde Kelani

Start with Tunde Kelani if you want to see where modern Nigerian cinema found its literary and cultural roots. Trained at the London Film School after cutting his teeth in photography and television, the Mainframe Films founder has spent decades turning Nigerian literature, stage plays, and history into lasting screen works.

Titles like Ti Oluwa Nile, Koseegbe, O Le Ku, Saworoide, Thunderbolt: Magun, The Narrow Path, Maami, Dazzling Mirage, Ayinla, and Cordelia show how wide his range goes. Across years of festivals and awards, Kelani has collected major honours for his craft, and his adaptation Cordelia earned him a Best Director nomination at the 2026 Africa Magic Viewers’ Choice Awards.

Tunde Kelani, whose directing catalogue spans Ti Oluwa Nile, Saworoide, The Narrow Path, Maami, and Cordelia, with Kunle Afolayan outdoors. Photo Credit: Tunde Kelani/Instagram

Akinola Davies Jr.

Few directors have linked global festival stages with homegrown Nollywood triumphs quite like Akinola Davies Jr. After his short film Lizard won the Short Film Grand Jury Prize at the Sundance Film Festival in 2021, he co-wrote and directed his feature debut My Father’s Shadow alongside his brother Wale Davies.

The drama made history in 2025 as the first Nigerian film selected for the Official Selection at the Cannes Film Festival, picking up a Special Mention for the Caméra d’Or before winning Best Director at the British Independent Film Awards and Breakthrough Director at the Gotham Independent Film Awards. His momentum rolled straight into 2026 with a BAFTA win for Outstanding Debut by a British Writer, Director or Producer, followed by Best Director and Best Overall Movie wins at the 2026 AMVCAs.

Akinola Davies Jr. with his BAFTA trophy for My Father’s Shadow. Photo Credit: Akinola Davies Jr./Instagram

Kemi Adetiba

Before crossing into cinema and streaming, Kemi Adetiba built a reputation directing memorable music videos for artists including Wizkid, Tiwa Savage, Olamide, and Banky W.

On the big screen, she shattered box-office records with The Wedding Party and followed up with the crime drama King of Boys, its sequel King of Boys: The Return of the King, and the series To Kill a Monkey. Her sharp pacing, bold casting, and distinct visual style have kept her in the spotlight across platforms such as The Headies, the City People Entertainment Awards, and the AMVCAs.

Kemi Adetiba and Bucci Franklin on the set of To Kill a Monkey. Photo Credit: Kemi Adetiba/Instagram

Daniel Etim Effiong

Many movie lovers know Daniel Etim Effiong first as a familiar leading man across Nollywood films and streaming hits, yet his work behind the camera is just as central to his career.

Having studied filmmaking at AFDA in South Africa and gained experience on shorts and television episodes, he stepped into feature directing with the thriller The Herd. That debut brought him Best Director and Best Debut Feature Film by a Director nominations at the 2026 Africa Movie Academy Awards, while The Herd collected three AMAA trophies and earned nine AMVCA nominations, including Best Director.

Daniel Etim Effiong on the set of The Herd which leads the 12th AMVCA nominations with 9 nods including Best Director.

Dammy Twitch

Known for years for directing visually bold music videos for stars like Davido, Burna Boy, and Omah Lay, Dammy Twitch (Apampa Oluwadamilola Owolabi) made his feature film directing debut in May 2026 with the romantic comedy Call of My Life.

Led by Uzoamaka Power and Andrew Yaw Bunting alongside Zubby Michael, Beverly Osu, Nkem Owoh, Patience Ozokwor, and Broda Shaggi, the film crossed ₦900 million at the Nigerian box office to become one of the highest-grossing Nollywood releases of 2026, while also winning the Favourite Feature Narrative Audience Award at the 2026 BlackStar Film Festival. Bringing his instincts for framing, colour, and pacing from music visuals into narrative cinema, he has quickly become a fresh voice movie fans are keeping a close eye on.

Dammy Twitch on the set of Call of My Life. Photo Credit: Dammy Twitch/Instagram
